title: Roots of unity as a finite group
section: Part B: Abstract Algebra ▷ Examples of Groups

question.text:
84 126
How many complex numbers satisfy both z = 1 and z = 1?
(A) 14 (B) 21 (C) 28 (D) 42 (E) 84

solution.text:
The common roots are precisely the gcd(84, 126) = 42 roots of unity of order dividing 42.
42
Bezout also shows the two equations imply z = 1.

question.text:
14 2πi/30
How many elements z ∈ U satisfy z = e ?
60
(A) 0 (B) 1 (C) 2 (D) 14 (E) 30

solution.text:
2πik/60
Write z = e . The equation is 14k ≡ 2 (mod 60), equivalent to 7k ≡ 1 (mod 30).
Since seven is a unit modulo thirty, this determines one class there and two classes modulo
sixty, namely k = 13, 43. Both correspond to valid elements of the specified group.

question.text:
If u and v are each primitive eighth roots of unity, which list gives all possible orders of uv?
(A) 8 only (B) 4 only (C) 2 or 4 only (D) 1, 2, or 4 (E) 1, 2, 4, or 8

solution.text:
a b
Write u = ζ , v = ζ for a primitive eighth root ζ. The primitive exponents are the four
odd residues 1, 3, 5, 7, in agreement with φ(8) = 4. Their sum is even, so the product has
order dividing four. Taking exponent pairs (1, 7), (1, 3), (1, 1) gives orders one, two, and
four respectively.
